Life tables from death rates on any age axis

Source: R/derive-lifetable.R
life_table.Rd

Period life table for single or grouped ages with an open last interval. Interval widths come from the age axis, so abridged and single-year schedules are handled by the same code.

Usage

life_table(
  mx,
  age = NULL,
  ax = NULL,
  open = c("reciprocal", "gompertz", "kannisto"),
  k = 10,
  radix = 1e+05
)

Arguments

mx

Death rates, one per interval of age.

age

An mt_axis (default: single ages from 0 with an open last interval).

ax

Optional average years lived in the interval by those who die.

open

"reciprocal", "gompertz" or "kannisto".

k

Number of ages used for the Gompertz fit.

radix

Starting number of survivors.

Value

A data.table with age_lo, age_hi, n, mx, ax, qx, lx, dx, Lx, Tx, ex.

Details

  • q_x = n m / (1 + (n - a) m); where this exceeds 1 (rates above about 2 / n, far beyond observed values), the constant-hazard value 1 - exp(-n m) is used, so that survivors stay positive;

  • a_x defaults to n / 2 for every closed interval (supply ax to override, for example for age 0, where n / 2 overstates the average time lived by infants who die; the effect on e0 at low infant mortality is below 0.01 years);

  • open interval: "reciprocal" uses L = l / m; "gompertz" fits a Gompertz line to the log rates of the last k closed single-year ages and integrates it from the start of the open interval to age 130; "kannisto" does the same with the Kannisto model, a line for the logit of the rates, whose hazard levels off at old ages (Thatcher, Kannisto and Vaupel 1998);

  • a rate of 0 in the open interval (no deaths, as in small populations) would give an infinite life expectancy: the last positive rate of the closed intervals is used for the open interval instead (column mx keeps the given rate). Only a schedule without any positive rate gives an infinite value.

References

Thatcher AR, Kannisto V, Vaupel JW (1998). The Force of Mortality at Ages 80 to 120. Odense University Press.

Examples

m <- 3e-4 + 2e-5 * exp(0.1 * (30:100))
lt <- life_table(m, single_ages(30, 100))
lt[age_lo %in% c(30, 65, 100)]
#>    age_lo age_hi     n           mx       ax           qx         lx         dx

#> 3:    100    Inf   Inf 0.4408293159 2.268452 1.0000000000   1460.141 1460.14118
#>          Lx         Tx        ex
#>       <num>      <num>     <num>
#> 1: 99964.93 4973452.39 49.734524
